books.section: Topic 4.6 Market Revolution: Society and Culture, A. Migrations and New Communities in the Age of the Market Revolution

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Barron’s Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.6 A: More than four million Americans crossed the Appalachian Mountains between 1800 and 1840 to settle in the West. Many Southern planters moved into Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Arkansas, and later Texas, hoping to recreate the Cotton Kingdom, complete with slave labor, on cheaper land. Farmers from the upper South moved into southern Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois, while New England and New York families settled in northern Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois, as well as Wisconsin and Michigan. Over time, the towns and churches of the Old Northwest began to resemble New England, while the plantations of the newly settled South resembled the Old South. Meanwhile, most immigrants who arrived between 1800 and 1860 came from northern and western Europe. Four-fifths of Irish immigrants settled in port cities of the Northeast, while German immigrants, often with more money, moved on to the “German triangle” of Cincinnati, St. Louis, and Milwaukee.
stimulus.source_note: Secondary text: paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.6 A. Paraphrased, not quoted.

options.text: weakened slavery by spreading it too thin
options.misconception: Moving planters west strengthened slavery by giving it new land, not by weakening it.

options.text: was driven mainly by German immigrants
options.misconception: German immigrants settled in the German triangle of Midwestern cities; the planters moving into Alabama and Mississippi were Southerners.

options.text: spread slavery and the plantation system into new lands
ended the movement of enslaved people from the upper South
options.misconception: The move west increased the internal slave trade, as enslaved people were carried or sold into the new cotton lands.

rationales.A: New cotton land made slavery more profitable, not weaker. Expansion gave the system room to grow.
rationales.B: The planters were Southerners moving into Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana. German immigrants went to Midwestern cities, not to the cotton frontier.
rationales.C: Planters moved west to recreate the Cotton Kingdom, complete with slave labor, on cheaper land. Expansion carried the plantation system into Alabama, Mississippi, and beyond instead of ending it.
rationales.D: The internal slave trade grew with the move west. Enslaved people were carried and sold into the new cotton states.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what the planters wanted. To recreate the Cotton Kingdom, complete with slave labor.
2. Ask what that means for slavery. The system moves west with them, onto cheaper land.
3. Judge the direction. Expansion spread slavery; it did not leave it behind.
Background: As cotton spread, so did slavery and the internal slave trade, tying the South's wealth ever more tightly to enslaved labor.
Remember: when people move to rebuild a system, the system moves with them.
